analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from forcing servicemembers into arbitration instead of court after a dispute arises.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and its Economic Opportunity Subcommittee in August 2023 and died there when the Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, the law that gives active-duty troops special legal protections, so that companies could no longer use pre-signed arbitration clauses to keep servicemembers out of court. Under the bill, arbitration could only be used if the servicemember agreed in writing after the actual dispute arose. It also would have tightened rules on waivers of servicemembers' rights and clarified that servicemembers can sue in court regardless of prior agreements.
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty servicemembers and their spouses. When a lender, landlord, or other company violates their rights under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act — for example, by charging illegal interest rates or repossessing property without a court order — the bill would let them take the case to court instead of being funneled into a private arbitration process chosen by the company. Arbitration proceedings are typically confidential, decided by a private arbitrator, and offer little chance to appeal, so the practical effect would be to restore troops' day-in-court rights.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a written-consent requirement to the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act: arbitration of a dispute covered by the Act could proceed only if, after the dispute arises, all parties consent in writing [S2]. This would end the common practice of burying forced-arbitration clauses in car loans, credit cards, leases, and phone contracts that servicemembers sign before deployment.
It applies to any contract with a servicemember, or a servicemember and spouse jointly, and covers contracts entered into, amended, renewed, or extended after enactment [S2].

The bill narrows waivers of SCRA rights: a servicemember could only waive the Act's protections after a specific dispute has arisen and that dispute is identified in the waiver, blocking blanket waivers signed at the time of the contract [S2].

It clarifies the private right of action so a servicemember may bring a civil suit under the SCRA 'notwithstanding any previous agreement to the contrary,' reinforcing that contract clauses cannot strip them of their right to sue [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders, landlords, telecom companies, auto dealers, and other businesses that write arbitration clauses into contracts with servicemembers. They would lose a tool that typically reduces their litigation costs and lowers the odds of large judgments or class actions, and they would face more court cases — including class actions — over violations of servicemembers' legal protections. Public court dockets, not private arbitrators, would absorb these disputes.

drawbacks.text: Companies facing SCRA claims could no longer steer them into arbitration, so they would bear the higher costs of open-court litigation — filing fees, discovery, trials, and potential class actions — costs that businesses argue can be passed along to customers through prices and credit terms.

The bill's one-sentence description says 'for other purposes,' but the introduced text contains only the arbitration, waiver, and private-right-of-action provisions; there is no dedicated funding or enforcement mechanism beyond the existing private right of action, so a servicemember would still need a lawyer and time — scarce resources for a deployed service member — to actually use these rights.

The provisions apply only to contracts entered into or amended after enactment, and to waivers made after enactment, so servicemembers already stuck in contracts with forced-arbitration clauses would get no help [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For servicemembers, the benefit is real: the SCRA already gives them strong substantive rights, but those rights can be neutralized when a company forces the dispute into arbitration that the company chose and controls. The cost falls on businesses that would face more litigation, some of which may be passed to consumers generally. The main design weakness is that it offers no help for disputes already locked into arbitration clauses and adds no new enforcement help for troops.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, passed along to a subcommittee three weeks later, and never came back out — no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on August 1, 2023, as a standalone bill with no cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Veterans' Affairs Committee on the day of introduction, and on August 24, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, where it remained [S4].
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that use arbitration clauses in contracts with servicemembers — lenders, landlords, and telecom and finance companies — keep the status quo: they can continue resolving SCRA disputes in private arbitration rather than court. Servicemembers gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies using arbitration clauses against troops

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no bipartisan coalition ever formed around it [S3].

industries.industry: Consumer lenders, credit card issuers, and auto finance companies
industries.note: These companies commonly place forced-arbitration clauses in loans to servicemembers and are frequent defendants in SCRA cases over illegal interest charges and repossessions. The bill would have forced their disputes with troops into public court.

Service contracts and leases routinely include arbitration clauses and broad waivers; the bill would have made those clauses and waivers unenforceable against servicemembers, opening them to court suits.
Arbitration providers earn fees from the disputes companies route to them; a ban on pre-dispute arbitration clauses covering servicemembers would shrink that business.
